about.title: Crescent City Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Crescent City's economy runs on fishing docks, logging operations, retail along 5th Street, and the steady flow of trucking and delivery traffic on US-101. Workers in these jobs face real risks — falls, vehicle collisions, and equipment accidents among them. In most cases, California workers' compensation is the only path against your employer, no matter who was at fault. But if a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to your injury, you may also have a separate claim against that third party. This matters in Del Norte County, where many worksites involve outside contractors and shared equipment. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we're a free service that connects injured workers with an independent attorney who can look at both sides of your situation: the workers' comp claim and any potential third-party case. There's no cost unless your attorney recovers money for you.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Work Injury Claim

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: California generally treats workers' comp as the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party — like a subcontractor or equipment maker — can still be held separately liable.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and missing that window can complicate your claim, so getting guidance early helps protect your options.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from punishing you for reporting an injury or filing a claim, and an attorney can help you understand your protections if you're worried about retaliation.

items.question: I was hurt while making a delivery on US-101 in Crescent City. Is that a workers' comp case or something else?
items.answer: It could be both. If you were on the job when it happened, workers' comp likely applies to your employer, but if another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate third-party injury claim. An attorney can look at the details and explain which paths are available to you.

items.question: How long do I have to report my injury to my employer?
items.answer: California generally requires you to notify your employer within 30 days of a workplace injury. Reporting later can make it harder to establish your claim, so it's best to report as soon as you're able.

items.question: Can my employer fire me for filing a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: No — California law makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against you for reporting a work injury or filing a claim. If you believe you've faced retaliation, an attorney can help you understand your options.
